concepts.name: Definition of Intangible Cultural Heritage under Article 2 of the 2003 Convention
key_dimensions: Five enumerated domains: oral traditions, performing arts, social practices, knowledge of nature/universe, traditional craftsmanship — and what is excluded
The 'community, groups, individuals' triad vs. state-centric ownership — a common UPSC trap on who 'holds' ICH
Distinction between ICH and tangible cultural heritage (World Heritage Sites under 1972 Convention) — overlap and boundary cases
The qualifier 'compatible with existing human rights instruments' — why this filters out certain practices

concepts.name: The Five Domains of ICH — Scope, Overlap, and Edge Cases
key_dimensions: Oral traditions and expressions including language as a vehicle (not language itself) — a subtle but exam-worthy distinction
Traditional craftsmanship as the most 'tangible' of the five domains — why it is still classified as ICH
Social practices, rituals, and festive events vs. performing arts — how UPSC questions conflate these two domains
Knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe — connection to traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) and biodiversity frameworks like CBD

concepts.name: Three UNESCO Lists under the 2003 Convention — Representative List, Urgent Safeguarding List, and Register of Good Safeguarding Practices
key_dimensions: Representative List of ICH of Humanity (RL) vs. List of ICH in Need of Urgent Safeguarding (USL) — criteria differences and Indian inscriptions on each
Register of Best Safeguarding Practices — least discussed but appears in MCQs as a trap ('fourth list' distractors)
Common misconception: inscription on RL does NOT imply 'endangered' status — UPSC frequently exploits this
A single element can appear on only one list at a time — the transfer mechanism from RL to USL

concepts.name: Criteria R.1–R.5 for Inscription on the Representative List
key_dimensions: R.1: The element must constitute ICH as defined in Article 2 — circularity trap in MCQs
R.2: Inscription must contribute to visibility and awareness of ICH in general, NOT just safeguard the specific element — a counterintuitive criterion
R.3: Safeguarding measures must be developed — measures are required at nomination stage, not post-inscription
R.4: Free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) of the community — alignment with indigenous rights frameworks; R.5: Involvement of the community in the nomination process itself

concepts.name: Criteria U.1–U.5 for Inscription on the Urgent Safeguarding List
key_dimensions: U.1: Element must meet Article 2 definition AND face serious threats — the additional 'viability threat' burden not required for RL
U.2: Urgent safeguarding measures are required — states must demonstrate a concrete safeguarding plan at the time of filing
Distinction: USL inscription IS a distress signal unlike RL; implications for international assistance and funding from the ICH Fund
India's Kutiyattam Sanskrit Theatre (2008, USL transfer to RL trajectory) — case study on the transition mechanism

concepts.name: Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) Requirement in ICH Nominations
key_dimensions: FPIC as Criterion R.4/U.4 — who constitutes the 'community' for consent purposes when a practice spans multiple states or nations
Multi-state nominations: how consent is aggregated across communities in different countries (e.g., Yoga, Nawrouz)
Contrast with 1972 World Heritage Convention where state party consent is sufficient — ICH adds community layer
Cases where community consent was disputed post-inscription — ethical dimensions for Essay/Ethics papers

concepts.name: Role and Powers of the Intergovernmental Committee for ICH (IGC)
key_dimensions: Composition: 24 states elected by the General Assembly — not all UNESCO member states, a common error
IGC's power to inscribe, defer, refer back, or decline nominations — the 'refer back' option is most commonly tested
IGC vs. General Assembly of States Parties — division of powers (IGC manages lists; GA sets policy and elects IGC members)
The Subsidiary Body and Evaluation Body — the 2014 shift from Subsidiary Body to independent Evaluation Body for credibility

concepts.name: The ICH Fund — Financing Mechanism under Article 25
key_dimensions: Mandatory contributions (1% of UNESCO regular budget contribution) vs. voluntary contributions — sources of the Fund
Fund's priority use: capacity building in developing countries and supporting USL nominations — NOT general cultural promotion
International Assistance requests: threshold amounts and which body approves them (IGC for above USD 25,000; Bureau for below)
Contrast with World Heritage Fund under 1972 Convention — different thresholds and governance

concepts.name: India's Inscriptions on the Representative List — Pattern and Gaps
key_dimensions: Chronological progression: Kutiyattam (2008) → Vedic Chanting → Ramlila → Ramman → Chhau → Kalbelia → Mudiyettu → Ladakhi Buddhist chants → Sankirtana → Yoga → Nawrouz (shared) → Kumbh Mela → Durga Puja → Garba — sequencing MCQs
Joint/multinational inscriptions India is part of: Nawrouz (shared with 12 countries) — implications for 'ownership'
What is NOT inscribed yet despite nominations — Jhumur, Thatheras craft (inscribed 2014) as a craftsmanship domain example
Thatheras of Jandiala Guru (2014) as the only craft tradition from India on RL — domain-specific trap question

concepts.name: Multinational/Joint Nominations — Rules and Strategic Implications
key_dimensions: Any number of states can jointly nominate a single element — no ceiling, unlike World Heritage Site co-nominations
Each co-nominating state gets 'credit' on their national count — strategic motivation for joining multinational files
Nawrouz case: 12 co-nominating countries spanning Central Asia, Middle East, South Asia — tests knowledge of geographic spread
Dispute mechanism when countries claim exclusive ownership of a joint element (e.g., Yoga-related practices)

concepts.name: Periodicity and Reporting Obligations of States Parties
key_dimensions: States must submit periodic reports to IGC every six years on the status of RL elements on their territory
USL elements require more frequent reporting — every four years — a testable numerical difference
Reports feed into IGC's decision to retain, transfer, or remove an element from a list
India's compliance record and the mechanism for removal of an element (rarely tested but high-yield for Mains)

concepts.name: Relationship between 2003 ICH Convention and 1972 World Heritage Convention
key_dimensions: 1972 Convention: tangible heritage (monuments, sites, natural landscapes) with Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) criterion
2003 Convention: intangible heritage with community-centricity, no 'OUV' concept — this absence is a deliberate policy choice
An element can have both tangible and intangible dimensions (e.g., Kumbh Mela infrastructure vs. ritual practices) — dual listing possibility
The 2003 Convention explicitly rejects 'hierarchy' among cultures — contrast with OUV's implicit hierarchy in 1972

concepts.name: The 'Safeguarding' Concept — Definition and Measures under Article 2(3)
key_dimensions: Safeguarding defined as: identification, documentation, research, preservation, protection, promotion, enhancement, transmission, revitalization
Distinction between 'preservation' (freezing) and 'revitalization' (allowing evolution) — ICH explicitly favors living, evolving practices
States parties' obligations: inventory-making is mandatory (Article 12), not optional — a frequently tested point
India's National Inventory of ICH vs. UNESCO list — the two are independent; domestic inventory does not guarantee UNESCO inscription

concepts.name: Inventorying Obligation under Article 12 — National Inventories
key_dimensions: Article 12 mandates that each state party draw up national inventories — this is a binding obligation, not discretionary
Inventories must be regularly updated — no fixed periodicity specified in the Convention text (trap: don't confuse with reporting periods)
India's nodal agency: Sangeet Natak Akademi maintains the national ICH inventory — institutional knowledge for Mains
Inventories are a precondition for nomination but are NOT sufficient — additional criteria must be met for inscription

concepts.name: Role of NGOs and Communities vs. State Parties in ICH Governance
key_dimensions: NGOs with recognized competence can be admitted as observers to IGC — accreditation process and distinction from state observer status
Communities are nominators in spirit but not formally — states submit nominations on behalf of communities (sovereignty trap)
Article 15: states shall endeavor to ensure widest possible participation of communities — 'endeavor' is non-binding language, unlike mandatory inventory obligation
Tension between state control of nominations and community self-determination — Ethics paper angle

concepts.name: Entry into Force, Ratification, and India's Accession to the 2003 Convention
key_dimensions: Convention adopted: October 17, 2003; entered into force: April 20, 2006 (after 30 ratifications) — numerical trap
India ratified the 2003 Convention in 2005 — making it among the early ratifiers
Contrast: India has also ratified the 1972 Convention — dual membership and obligations
The Convention requires 30 ratifications to enter into force — compare with other UNESCO conventions (1972 required 20)

concepts.name: Kumbh Mela Inscription (2017) — Case Study on Scale and Community Consent
key_dimensions: Inscribed under 'Social practices, rituals and festive events' domain — domain identification is a standard MCQ
Kumbh Mela as a periodic event (not continuous practice) — how ICH handles cyclical rather than continuous elements
FPIC complexity: consent from millions of pilgrims — how India addressed this in nomination file
Post-inscription obligations: India's reporting on safeguarding measures for an event of this scale

concepts.name: Yoga Inscription (2016) — Geopolitical and Definitional Controversies
key_dimensions: Inscribed under 'Social practices, rituals and festive events' AND 'knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe' — dual domain classification
Pakistan's objection during nomination process — how IGC handles inter-state disputes over nominations
Distinction between Yoga as ICH (practice, transmission, community) vs. Yoga as intellectual property — ICH inscription confers no IP rights
India's 'soft power' use of ICH inscriptions — Ethics and Essay angle on instrumentalization of cultural heritage

concepts.name: Removal and De-inscription of ICH Elements — Article 35 and IGC Powers
key_dimensions: An element can be removed if the state party requests it, or if it no longer meets inscription criteria — two distinct removal triggers
IGC has the power to remove an element from a list following the reporting mechanism — rarely exercised but theoretically important
No element has been formally de-inscribed from RL as of 2024 — but elements have been transferred between lists
Contrast with World Heritage 'In Danger' list and de-listing (e.g., Dresden Elbe Valley) — ICH has no equivalent 'in danger' list beyond USL

concepts.name: Comparison: 2003 ICH Convention vs. 2005 Convention on Cultural Diversity
key_dimensions: 2003 Convention: safeguarding specific intangible practices; 2005 Convention: protecting diversity of cultural expressions in trade and media contexts
2005 Convention targets cultural industries and creative economies — not traditional/community practices per se
Both conventions share the anti-homogenization principle but operate in different domains — UPSC conflates these in statement-based MCQs
India's ratification status: India ratified both — but 2005 Convention has direct implications for WTO trade negotiations in cultural sectors
